title: Climbing the rungs
hookLine: Maimonides' eight levels of giving, lived
tomorrow: Owen's church serves a free dinner. why does Noa think of a field?

cards: A fundraising page loads with its scrolling list: names, amounts, little hearts, a progress bar. Some gifts say anonymous. Some names are in bold.
Is one of those better than the others, or is a check a check? Maimonides built a ladder for exactly this question, eight rungs of tzedakah, in his code of law, the Mishneh Torah.
Read it from the bottom, and the bottom rung is a surprise: it still counts. Giving grudgingly, with a sour face, is a rung. Above it, giving cheerfully but less than you should.
Then giving after you're asked. Then before.

teach.b: Higher up, the rungs are about faces: who knows whom. The giver knows the receiver, but the receiver doesn't know the giver. Then the other way around.

Then neither knows the other, like the chamber in the Temple where, the code says, people left gifts in secret and poor families drew from it in secret. Plenty of people stop there and call anonymous giving the top.

teach.h: THE TOP: A HAND BEFORE THE FALL.
teach.b: The top rung is taking hold of someone's hand before they fall: a gift, a loan, a partnership, or finding them work, so they won't need to ask anyone again. Every rung below the top still leaves someone receiving.
The top one ends the need.

teach.h: ONE STEP UP, NOT A SCORECARD.
teach.b: Lived, the ladder is less a scorecard than a next step. If you give when asked, try giving before.
If your name is always on it, try once without. And when someone near you is close to falling, a job lead, an introduction, or a loan with no shame in it may do more than a check.
Something to tell a friend tonight: on Maimonides' ladder, helping someone get hired sits above the anonymous donation.

how: Many Jews know Maimonides' eight levels of tzedakah from school or synagogue study; communities put the top rung into practice through free-loan societies, job networks and small-business help.

games.q: a neighbor lost his job and is too proud to take charity. you could slip him an anonymous gift, or connect him with a manager who's hiring. which is higher on the ladder?
o: the introduction: work is the top rung, so he won't need to ask.
the anonymous gift: not knowing who gave is the very top.
neither: until he asks, the mitzvah doesn't apply.
games.why: the top rung is strengthening someone before they fall, including finding them work. the anonymous gift is a fine rung, just not the highest.

practice: Bring to mind the last thing you gave, and find its rung: asked or unasked, named or quiet, a gift or a hand up. Then, with the next few breaths, move it one rung higher and see what the same gift would look like there.
Let that one picture stay with you.

wordCard.voice: Climbing the rungs: Maimonides' eight ways to give, from grudging at the bottom to a hand up at the top, taken one step at a time.

orig.note: Hebrew: giving to the poor; Maimonides' ladder is a ladder of tzedakah.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: one rung higher, not the whole ladder at once. Five days into community and justice.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Gifts to the Poor 10:7–14 (the eight levels of tzedakah; the secret chamber in the Temple at 10:8)
